courses.title: Histopathology and Cytopathology Techniques
courses.description: Advanced tissue processing, special stains, immunohistochemistry, frozen sections, diagnostic cytology and cervical screening, and laboratory quality in cellular pathology.

topics.title: Advanced Tissue Processing and Microtomy
topics.summary: Specimen reception, fixation problems, processing schedules, embedding and section artefacts.

material.heading: From specimen to block
material.body: Specimens must arrive correctly labelled with a completed request form (patient details, clinical history, specimen type); mismatches are rejected or resolved before processing. Adequate fixation in 10% neutral buffered formalin needs about 10–20 times the tissue volume and sufficient time (formalin penetrates about 1 mm per hour but fixes more slowly); large specimens are opened or sliced. Under-fixation causes poor morphology and antigen loss; delayed fixation (cold ischaemia time > 1 hour) degrades antigens — critical for breast cancer hormone receptor and HER2 testing (fixation 6–72 hours). Formalin pigment (acid formaldehyde haematin) forms in acidic or blood-rich tissue — removed with alcoholic picric acid. Automated processors take tissue through dehydration (graded alcohols), clearing (xylene or substitutes) and infiltration (molten paraffin wax at about 56–60 °C). Embedding orientation matters (e.g. skin and gut walls on edge, cysts to show wall).

material.heading: Microtomy and artefacts
material.body: Rotary microtomes cut paraffin sections at about 3–5 µm; sections are floated on a water bath (about 5–10 °C below wax melting point) and picked up on (adhesive-coated) slides. Decalcification of bone uses acids (formic acid — slower but gentler; nitric acid — rapid but damaging) or chelating agents (EDTA — slow, preserves morphology and DNA/antigens); the end-point is tested chemically or radiographically. Common artefacts: chatter (vibration — lines parallel to the knife edge; tissue too hard or loose blade), scoring/lines perpendicular to the knife edge (nicks in the blade), holes (over-dehydrated, brittle tissue), thick-and-thin sections (loose block or clamp), folds and bubbles, and 'floaters' (contaminating tissue from the water bath — a serious diagnostic risk). Frozen sections using a cryostat (about −20 °C) give rapid intraoperative diagnosis (margins, malignancy) within about 20 minutes.

topics.title: Special Stains
topics.summary: Carbohydrates, connective tissue, microorganisms, pigments and amyloid.

material.heading: Carbohydrates and connective tissue
material.body: Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stains glycogen, neutral mucins, basement membranes and fungi magenta; diastase digestion (PAS-D) removes glycogen, confirming it. Alcian blue stains acid mucins (pH 2.5 — carboxylated and sulfated; pH 1.0 — sulfated only); combined Alcian blue/PAS distinguishes mucin types (e.g. intestinal metaplasia in Barrett's oesophagus). Mucicarmine stains epithelial mucin and the capsule of Cryptococcus. Connective tissue stains: Masson's trichrome (collagen blue/green, muscle red — liver fibrosis), van Gieson (collagen red, muscle yellow), Verhoeff–van Gieson or elastic stains (elastic fibres black — vessels), reticulin (silver impregnation of type III collagen fibres black — liver architecture, tumour patterns), and Perls' Prussian blue for haemosiderin (ferric iron blue — iron overload).
keyPoints: PAS: glycogen, fungi; PAS-D confirms glycogen

material.heading: Microorganisms and others
material.body: Ziehl–Neelsen (ZN) stain demonstrates acid-fast bacilli (Mycobacterium tuberculosis red; Wade–Fite modification for M. leprae); Gram stain in tissue (Brown–Hopps, Brown–Brenn); Grocott's methenamine silver (GMS) stains fungi black (Pneumocystis, Aspergillus, Histoplasma); Giemsa for Helicobacter and parasites (Leishmania); Warthin–Starry silver for spirochaetes. Congo red stains amyloid, giving apple-green birefringence under polarised light (diagnostic). Fat stains (Oil Red O, Sudan black) need frozen sections because processing dissolves lipid. Masson–Fontana demonstrates melanin (black); melanin bleaching distinguishes it from other pigments. Von Kossa stains calcium salts black. Controls (known positive tissue) must be run with every special stain.
keyPoints: ZN: AFB red; Wade–Fite for leprosy

topics.title: Immunohistochemistry and Molecular Histopathology
topics.summary: IHC principles, antigen retrieval, detection systems, key markers and in situ hybridisation.

material.heading: IHC technique
material.body: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) uses antibodies to localise antigens in tissue sections. Formalin fixation masks epitopes through protein cross-links; heat-induced epitope retrieval (HIER — heating sections in citrate pH 6 or EDTA/Tris pH 9 buffers) or enzyme digestion (proteinase K, trypsin) restores antigenicity. Steps: dewax and rehydrate, retrieval, block endogenous peroxidase (hydrogen peroxide) and non-specific binding, primary antibody (monoclonal — specific; polyclonal — sensitive), polymer-based detection system (e.g. HRP-labelled polymer), chromogen (DAB — brown, permanent; AEC — red, alcohol-soluble), and haematoxylin counterstain. Controls: positive and negative tissue controls, and internal controls. Automated stainers improve reproducibility.
keyPoints: HIER: citrate pH 6 or EDTA pH 9

material.heading: Diagnostic markers
material.body: IHC panels identify tumour lineage: cytokeratins (AE1/AE3 — carcinoma; CK7/CK20 patterns suggest the primary site: CK7+/CK20− lung, breast; CK7−/CK20+ colorectal), vimentin (mesenchymal), LCA/CD45 (lymphoma; CD20 B cells, CD3 T cells), S100, SOX10, HMB-45 and Melan-A (melanoma), desmin and myogenin (rhabdomyosarcoma), CD34 and CD31 (vascular tumours; CD34 in Kaposi sarcoma with HHV-8 LANA-1 — common in HIV-positive Nigerians), TTF-1 (lung and thyroid), PSA (prostate), and Ki-67 (proliferation index). Predictive markers in breast cancer: ER, PR (Allred or H-score) and HER2 (scored 0–3+; 2+ equivocal cases are resolved by in situ hybridisation — FISH or chromogenic ISH — for HER2 gene amplification). Burkitt lymphoma (endemic in African children) shows CD10, BCL6 and Ki-67 near 100% with MYC translocation.
keyPoints: CD45 lymphoma; CD20 B; CD3 T

topics.title: Diagnostic Cytopathology
topics.summary: Exfoliative and aspiration cytology, FNAC, fluid cytology, preparation and staining.

material.heading: Specimen types
material.body: Cytopathology studies cells rather than tissue architecture. Exfoliative cytology examines cells shed naturally or scraped (cervical smears, sputum, urine, serous effusions); fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) samples palpable or image-guided lesions (thyroid, breast, lymph nodes, salivary glands) with a fine needle (22–25 gauge) — quick, cheap and minimally invasive, widely used in Nigerian hospitals. Rapid on-site evaluation (ROSE) checks adequacy. Fluids (pleural, peritoneal, CSF, urine) are centrifuged or cytospun; cell blocks (clotted sediment processed like tissue) allow IHC. Limitations: cannot always assess invasion; sampling errors cause false negatives; results reported in categories (e.g. Bethesda system for thyroid: I non-diagnostic to VI malignant; Milan system for salivary gland; Paris system for urine).

material.heading: Preparation and staining
material.body: Smears may be air-dried (for Romanowsky stains such as May–Grünwald–Giemsa or Diff-Quik — good cytoplasmic detail, rapid) or wet-fixed immediately in 95% ethanol (for Papanicolaou stain — excellent nuclear detail and cytoplasmic keratinisation; delays cause air-drying artefact). The Papanicolaou stain uses haematoxylin (nuclei), Orange G (keratin — orange) and EA (eosin–azure: light green for non-keratinised squamous cells, eosin for superficial cells). Liquid-based cytology (LBC — ThinPrep, SurePath) produces cleaner, thin-layer preparations with fewer unsatisfactory samples and allows HPV testing on the residual specimen. Features of malignancy: high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio, hyperchromasia, irregular nuclear membranes, coarse chromatin, prominent nucleoli, pleomorphism, abnormal mitoses and loss of cohesion.

topics.title: Cervical Screening and Quality in Cellular Pathology
topics.summary: Cervical cytology reporting, HPV testing, screening programmes and laboratory quality management.

material.heading: Cervical screening
material.body: Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer among Nigerian women and is largely preventable. High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV types 16 and 18 cause about 70%) drives progression through cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN 1–3) to invasive carcinoma over years. Screening approaches: Pap smear cytology (every 3 years), primary HPV DNA testing (every 5 years; WHO preferred), and visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA — low-resource, screen-and-treat). The Bethesda System for cervical cytology: NILM (negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy), ASC-US, ASC-H, LSIL (HPV effect/CIN 1 — koilocytes), HSIL (CIN 2–3), squamous cell carcinoma, and glandular abnormalities (AGC, adenocarcinoma in situ). Specimen adequacy requires sufficient squamous cells and ideally a transformation zone component (endocervical/metaplastic cells). WHO's 90-70-90 elimination targets: 90% of girls vaccinated, 70% of women screened, 90% treated.

material.heading: Quality management
material.body: Quality in cellular pathology includes: standard operating procedures, specimen tracking with unique identifiers (barcodes), turnaround time monitoring, internal quality control (control slides for each stain run, daily stain checks), rapid review or rescreening of negative cervical smears (e.g. 10% random or rapid review of all negatives) to detect false negatives, correlation of cytology with histology outcomes, audit, and participation in external quality assessment (EQA) schemes. Accreditation to ISO 15189 demonstrates competence. Health and safety: formalin (carcinogen — exposure monitoring, fume hoods), xylene (toxic, flammable — substitutes), sharp microtome blades, and infectious specimens (TB, prions — special handling). Proper disposal of chemical waste and tissue is required, and retention of blocks and slides follows national guidelines.
